The streamed-only condition of an outer join, which a `CASE WHEN` never reaches. A `ROLLUP`, and a split common subexpression. [SPARK-59674][CORE] Fix Comparison method violates its general contract in FIFOSchedulingAlgorithm

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`FIFOSchedulingAlgorithm.comparator` (used by `Pool.getSortedTaskSetQueue` to order `TaskSetManager`s/`Pool`s in FIFO scheduling mode) compared `priority` and `stageId` using:

```scala
math.signum(priority1 - priority2)
```

This subtraction can silently overflow when the two `Int` values are far apart (e.g. span `Int.MinValue`..`Int.MaxValue`), which flips the sign of the result and violates the `Comparator` contract (anti-symmetry/transitivity).

This PR replaces the subtraction-based `signum` comparisons with `Integer.compare`, which compares the two values directly and cannot overflow:

```scala
var res = Integer.compare(s1.priority, s2.priority)
if (res == 0) {
  res = Integer.compare(s1.stageId, s2.stageId)
}
```

### Why are the changes needed?

A broken comparator contract makes `java.util.TimSort` detect the inconsistency during the merge phase and throw, which surfaces as a driver-side failure when offering resources to executors:

```
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!
	at java.util.TimSort.mergeHi(TimSort.java:903)
	at java.util.TimSort.mergeAt(TimSort.java:520)
	at java.util.TimSort.mergeForceCollapse(TimSort.java:461)
	at java.util.TimSort.sort(TimSort.java:254)
	at java.util.Arrays.sort(Arrays.java:1233)
	at scala.collection.SeqLike.sorted(SeqLike.scala:659)
	...
	at org.apache.spark.scheduler.Pool.getSortedTaskSetQueue(Pool.scala:109)
	at org.apache.spark.scheduler.TaskSchedulerImpl.resourceOffers(TaskSchedulerImpl.scala:440)
	at org.apache.spark.scheduler.cluster.CoarseGrainedSchedulerBackend$DriverEndpoint.makeOffers(...)
```

Once this is thrown from `resourceOffers`, resource offers stop being processed correctly, which can stall task scheduling entirely. `Integer.compare` performs a purely logical comparison and does not have this overflow failure mode, so it satisfies the `Comparator` contract for any pair of `Int` values.

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This continues migrating the pandas UDF eval types onto the eval-handler framework (umbrella SPARK-59415), following `PandasScalarUDFHandler` (SPARK-59911) and the Arrow handler work. It moves two Batch-category iterator eval types off the `worker.py::read_udfs` if/elif chain onto handler classes in `python/pyspark/eval_handlers/_pandas.py`:

- `PandasScalarIterUDFHandler` for `SQL_SCALAR_PANDAS_ITER_UDF` -- the pandas counterpart of `ArrowScalarIterUDFHandler`: the UDF receives an iterator of its argument columns (struct columns as DataFrames), yields an iterator of pandas Series/DataFrames, and the handler enforces the declared element type, verifies the total row count matches the input, and converts each result back to one RecordBatch.
- `PandasMapUDFHandler` for `SQL_MAP_PANDAS_ITER_UDF` (mapInPandas) -- the pandas counterpart of `ArrowMapUDFHandler`: the UDF receives the input RecordBatch stream as an iterator of pandas DataFrames (one per batch, the single struct column expanded) and yields pandas DataFrames/Series, converted back to one RecordBatch each.

Both extend `BatchEvalTypeHandler` directly and call the Arrow<->pandas conversions in `pyspark.sql.conversion` (`ArrowToPandasConversion.to_pandas` / `PandasToArrowConversion.from_pandas`) inline with the runner_conf-derived parameters, exactly as `PandasScalarUDFHandler` does -- no pandas-specific intermediate base and no conversion wrappers, so each handler reads as a straight pandas analog of the Arrow one.

The class hierarchy after this PR (pandas mirrors Arrow -- both extend the category base directly):

```
EvalTypeHandler
  BatchEvalTypeHandler
    ArrowScalarIterUDFHandler      (SQL_SCALAR_ARROW_ITER_UDF, shipped)
    ArrowMapUDFHandler             (SQL_MAP_ARROW_ITER_UDF, shipped)
    PandasScalarUDFHandler         (SQL_SCALAR_PANDAS_UDF, shipped)
    PandasScalarIterUDFHandler     (SQL_SCALAR_PANDAS_ITER_UDF, new)
    PandasMapUDFHandler            (SQL_MAP_PANDAS_ITER_UDF, new)
```

The `SQL_SCALAR_PANDAS_ITER_UDF` and `SQL_MAP_PANDAS_ITER_UDF` branches are removed from `read_udfs` (both the serializer-selection entries and the mapper blocks); `read_udfs` now dispatches them through `get_eval_type_handler`, exactly as the migrated Arrow types already do. All other pandas branches are left untouched, and `read_single_udf` still handles both types (the handler path calls it).

`verify_pandas_result` and its helper `_verify_column_schema` move from `worker.py` into `pyspark/eval_handlers/verification.py`, where the other result-verification helpers already live, so the handlers can call them without importing `worker.py`. `worker.py` imports them back, so the remaining pandas branches and `verify_arrow_result` are unchanged.

### Why are the changes needed?

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Follow-up to [SPARK-59274](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59274). `from_json`, `from_csv`, `from_xml`, and `schema_of_*` take a STRING document. CHAR padding is part of the value after CAST to STRING (`LENGTH('abc'::CHAR(10)::STRING)` is 10 under `spark.sql.charVarchar.standardSemantics.enabled`). This PR removes `SupportTrimmedCharInput` so those functions no longer rtrim CHAR arguments.

Schema-driven parse of CHAR/VARCHAR *fields* from SPARK-59274 is unchanged: pad, overflow, and FAILFAST still apply to parsed output.

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59917

### Why are the changes needed?

These functions are STRING parsers. Special-casing CHAR by stripping trailing blanks disagrees with CAST-to-STRING semantics and with VARCHAR/STRING arguments, which keep trailing spaces.

In default mode, CHAR table columns are padded on read (`spark.sql.readSideCharPadding`, on by default) and reach these functions as padded STRINGs. The removed trait only matched first-class `CharType`, so on master `from_csv(char_col, ...)` could disagree depending on `spark.sql.charVarchar.standardSemantics.enabled`. This PR makes those paths agree.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, relative to current `master` (unreleased SPARK-59274). CHAR document arguments are no longer rtrimmed before parse.

JSON still accepts trailing whitespace, so a padded CHAR JSON document can still parse:

```sql
SELECT from_json(CAST('{"a":1}' AS CHAR(12)), 'a INT')
-- same result as
SELECT from_json('{"a":1}     ', 'a INT')
```

CSV makes the padding visible with a space delimiter. Extra empty fields are a token-count mismatch:

```sql
SELECT schema_of_csv(CAST('1' AS CHAR(3)), map('delimiter', ' '))
-- STRUCT<_c0: INT, _c1: STRING, _c2: STRING>

SELECT from_csv(CAST('1' AS CHAR(3)), '_c0 INT', map('delimiter', ' '))
-- PERMISSIVE still returns named_struct('_c0', 1)

SELECT from_csv(CAST('1' AS CHAR(3)), '_c0 INT', map('delimiter', ' ', 'mode', 'FAILFAST'))
-- MALFORMED_RECORD_IN_PARSING (previously parsed the trimmed value)
```

With the default comma delimiter, padding also lands on an unquoted last field, because `from_csv` and `schema_of_csv` keep trailing whitespace by default. Integral, decimal, and boolean converters reject those spaces; float and double accept them, so inference can fall through to DOUBLE:

```sql
SELECT schema_of_csv(CAST('1' AS CHAR(3)))
-- STRUCT<_c0: DOUBLE>  (was STRUCT<_c0: INT> after rtrim)

SELECT from_csv(CAST('1,2' AS CHAR(5)), 'a INT, b INT')
-- named_struct('a', 1, 'b', NULL)  (was {1, 2})

SELECT from_csv(CAST('1,ab' AS CHAR(6)), 'a INT, b STRING')
-- named_struct('a', 1, 'b', 'ab  ')

SELECT from_csv(
  CAST('1,2' AS CHAR(5)),
  'a INT, b INT',
  map('ignoreTrailingWhiteSpace', 'true'))
-- named_struct('a', 1, 'b', 2)
```

`map('ignoreTrailingWhiteSpace', 'true')` restores the trimmed last-field parse. FAILFAST on the INT last-field case raises `MALFORMED_RECORD_IN_PARSING`.

Default `spark.sql.charVarchar.standardSemantics.enabled` remains false. Released Spark versions are unchanged.

[SPARK-59954][SQL] Fix DECLARE VARIABLE failing on a NULLIF or BETWEEN default

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`RewriteWithExpression` pre-evaluates a common expression's definition in a `Project` over the first child whose output covers the definition's references. A default value references no column, so for a `CreateVariable` the rule put that `Project` over the first `ResolvedIdentifier`, which names a variable and is not an input. `V2CommandStrategy` plans a `CreateVariable` only when every child is a `ResolvedIdentifier`, so planning failed.

This adds a `CreateVariable` case to the rule. It inlines the definitions that gain nothing from memoizing, as it does for a `With` in a conditional branch, and leaves the rest in the default. `CreateVariableExec` evaluates the default on the driver, and a `With` can be evaluated since SPARK-58818, so a kept definition is evaluated once per `With`. A later rule that copies its input, such as `LikeSimplification` for a single pattern, copies the `With` too, and each copy evaluates the definition.

### Why are the changes needed?

```sql
DECLARE OR REPLACE VARIABLE v1 DOUBLE DEFAULT nullif(rand(), 0.5);
```

fails with

```
[INTERNAL_ERROR] The Spark SQL phase planning failed with an internal error. ... SQLSTATE: XX000
Caused by: java.lang.AssertionError: assertion failed: No plan for CreateVariable default(if ((_common_expr_0#0 = 0.5)) null else _common_expr_0#0) ...
+- Project [rand(...) AS _common_expr_0#0]
   +- ResolvedIdentifier ..., session.v1
```

`BETWEEN` fails the same way. Both wrap their first operand in a `With` that references it twice, so a NULLIF or BETWEEN default whose first operand is nondeterministic, like `rand()`, or not cheap to evaluate twice, like a Scala UDF, hits this. A cheap first operand, such as in `nullif(1, 3)`, is inlined and works.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. A DECLARE VARIABLE like the one above now creates the variable instead of failing with INTERNAL_ERROR.

### How was this patch tested?

- `RewriteWithExpressionSuite`: a `CreateVariable` whose default holds a `With` worth memoizing comes out of the rule unchanged, and one whose definition gains nothing is inlined.
- `ColumnExpressionSuite`: a NULLIF default and a BETWEEN default over a counting UDF each create the variable, call the UDF once, and read back the expected value. `nullif(rand(5), 0.5)`, a seeded form of the repro above, creates its variable.

Both fail without the change to `RewriteWithExpression`.

[SPARK-59696][SQL] Skip the redundant second modulo in integral MathUtils.pmod for positive divisors

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

For integral `MathUtils.pmod(a, n)` with `n > 0`, skip the redundant second modulo in the released `r = a % n; if (r < 0) (r + n) % n else r`. For `n > 0` the result is `Math.floorMod(a, n)`: a negative remainder only needs `n` added. This PR computes it with a branchless sign fix-up:

```scala
def pmod(a: Int, n: Int): Int = {
  val r = a % n
  if (n > 0) r + (n & (r >> 31)) else if (r >= 0) r else (r + n) % n
}
// Long: the same with `r >> 63`.
```

`n < 0` keeps the original `(r + n) % n`. `Byte`/`Short` delegate to `Int`. `Float`/`Double` are unchanged.

### Why are the changes needed?

`pmod` with a positive divisor is the common case (e.g. `HashPartitioning` passes `numPartitions` for every row), and the second `% n` is a no-op there.

The fix-up is written out because `Math.floorMod` adjusts with a data-dependent conditional, which C2 often keeps as a branch that mispredicts on random-sign dividends. JMH 1.37, x86_64, 16,384 `pmod(int, int)` calls per op over random-sign dividends, 3 forks x 10 iterations; us/op:

| divisor | JDK | released | `Math.floorMod` | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| JIT constant `200` | 17 | 20.5 | 31.9 (bimodal) | 14.9 |
| | 25 | 31.9 | 43.4 | 4.5 (*) |
| per-row `200` | 17 | 65.9 | 81.7 | 26.1 |
| | 25 | 70.7 | 40.6 | 26.2 |
| loop-invariant `200` | 17 | 89.0 | 42.2 | 26.1 |
| | 25 | 65.7 | 25.7 | 25.4 |

(*) Likely the benchmark loop vectorizing, which does not apply to per-row evaluation such as `HashPartitioning`. JDK 21 and ARM were not measured.

Harness (JMH and exhaustive equivalence check): https://gist.github.com/david-mollitor-db/1cc2fe01b478062efda9ec191efd0f51

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Results are identical for every input.

- `pmod(-7, 3)` via `testNumericDataTypes`, which exercises the integral `n > 0` fast path (`Byte`/`Short` via `Int`, and `Long`);
- `pmod(-6, 3) == 0` (`Int`, `Long`): a zero remainder with a negative dividend;
- a `Long` case whose remainder is below `-2^62`, so a wrong shift count or narrowing to `Int` changes the result;
- `pmod(-1e-20, 1.0) == 0.0` (and the `Float` analogue), which needs the float/double `% n`;

[SPARK-59620][SQL] Late-materialization storage-filter pushdown in the vectorized Parquet reader

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This adds a late-materialization read path to the vectorized Parquet reader, so the optimizer can hand a runtime filter to the scan and have it skip the IO for rows that filter rejects, instead of the filter running as a post-scan `FilterExec` over everything the scan read.

**What a storage filter is.** A predicate the scan is offered to read with, and is free not to honor, because it stays in the post-scan `Filter` as well. Today one shape qualifies, a top-level `BloomFilterMightContain` over columns of the scan's own projection, which is the runtime bloom `InjectRuntimeFilter` builds for a join. The columns it references are this reader's key columns.

**How it works**

Three phases per row group, all driven by one `ParquetFileReader` whose requested schema is switched between them.

- **Phase 0** narrows the row group to the rows the pushed data filters allow, through the column index. Metadata only, no page is read.
- **Phase 1** reads the key columns of those rows and evaluates the storage filter per row, keeping the surviving key values.
- **Phase 2** reads the remaining columns, restricted to the pages those surviving rows fall in. A row group with no survivor at all is skipped without reading a page of them at all, its key pages being what phase 1 already read.

Emit then splices each batch. The key columns come from what phase 1 kept, every other column from what phase 2 read.

Six things make the reader stop short of applying the filter, four of them once it is reading and the last two before it starts, on top of the shapes the planner declines. None of them changes an answer, because the storage filter is still in the post-scan `Filter`. What they cost is the saving, and each of the first four also reads the key columns a second time.

- the surviving rows of a row group scatter into more row ranges than the memory budget allows, so that row group is read with no filter applied;
- the buffered key values and those row ranges together pass that budget, so the buffer is released and phase 2 reads every projected column of the surviving rows instead, at the cost of reading the key columns twice;
- evaluating the filter, or decoding the key pages it is evaluated on, raises an error, so that row group is read with no filter applied. For an evaluation error the `Filter` then decides in its own order. Either a conjunct ahead of it drops the row before it runs, or it does not and the query fails the way it would have without this feature. A decode error meets the same page again, at the same batch a plain read would. A file missing every key column evaluates the filter once, on the values it reads those columns as, and an error there reads the whole file;
- the page index cannot be used to narrow a row group, so phase 2 reads every projected column and the filter is left with the row groups it empties. Three mechanisms reach it. A footer check per row group, over every projected column, which is what a file written with no page index answers for all of them. The conf `parquet.filter.columnindex.enabled` set to false, which says the index the file has is not to be trusted, and which closes phase 0 too, so nothing narrows by it at all. And parquet raising `MissingOffsetIndexException` from the read, which is the backstop for what the footer cannot see. Only that row group is read again, whole over the pushed data filter's ranges, so the rows that filter's own page pruning excludes stay excluded, and the other row groups are narrowed as usual;
- a file has none of the projected non-key leaves, so phase 2 would have nothing to read and the reader reads that file plainly;
- the vectorized reader turns out to be unavailable at execution time, so the read is plain from the start.

**Design decisions**

This is the first step of a longer effort, and it is deliberately narrow. It covers the v1 Parquet file source and the bloom filter `InjectRuntimeFilter` already produces. The steps after it are a DSv2 equivalent, so a connector such as Iceberg can prune the same way, and per-partition filters for a storage-partitioned join. All three share the goal here, a scan that is handed a runtime filter and uses it to decide what not to read, instead of reading everything and dropping rows above itself.

**A storage filter stays in the post-scan `Filter` as well.** The scan is offered it, not obliged to honor it, exactly as a pushed data filter works today. `FileSourceStrategy` removes only partition filters from the plan, because partition pruning is exact, and leaves the data filters it hands to Parquet in place, because statistics and column-index pruning are not. Late materialization is the second kind. DSv2 draws the same line from the other side, where a source returns the filters it cannot guarantee and `PushDownUtils` keeps those post-scan.

What that buys is the list above, a reader free to stop short whenever honoring the filter would cost more than it saves, or would raise an error the plan would not, with no correctness argument attached to any of it. It also means the bloom is never built for nothing, since the `Filter` uses it whatever the scan managed to do. Both sides read the same bytes, because the subquery that builds it is executed once, deduplicated by subquery reuse, with or without AQE. That is `spark.sql.execution.reuseSubquery`, on by default, and with it off the subquery runs for each side.

What it costs is evaluating the filter a second time for the rows the scan emits. Where the filter was applied those are the surviving rows, so the cost is proportional to what it kept rather than to what it discarded, and it is a hash and a few bit probes fused into the generated code. Where the reader stopped short they are all the rows the pushed data filters left, which is what the plan would have evaluated anyway.

So turning the conf on can cost a slower read of a row group the reader cannot prune, and outside the two cases below never a wrong answer. Nor a failed query, since any error from evaluating the filter that is not fatal gives that row group up, an `AssertionError` included. It is not narrowed to Spark's own errors, because a built-in expression can raise a plain JDK one, as `timestamp_seconds` of a decimal does from `longValueExact`. Nor to unchecked ones, because a Hive UDF in the key raises a checked `SparkException` (`FAILED_EXECUTE_UDF`) that nothing declares. Rethrowing has two bad ends and neither is the error the plan would have raised. The query fails where a plain read succeeds, and under `ignoreCorruptFiles` an exception from a reader is read as a corrupt file, which drops the rest of it silently. Two things are never absorbed, and both are asked the way the rest of Spark asks them. A pending task kill, which a UDF can surface as the interrupt it wrapped, is read off the task context. A fatal error in the cause chain is found by `Executor.isFatalError`. A fatal error at the top goes out as it is first, kill or no kill, as the executor checks it. A kill then goes out wrapped in a checked `SparkException`, since `ignoreCorruptFiles` would log a `RuntimeException` as a corrupt file and go on to the split's other files, and the executor still reports the task as killed. A fatal error deeper in the chain goes out as itself, found as deep as the executor would look had a plain plan raised the error, from the post-scan `Filter` for an evaluation error and from the reader for a decoding one. That is one level further down for a `NonFatal` decoding error, which `FileScanRDD` wraps before the executor looks. An `InternalError` from evaluation goes out in an `UnknownError`, another fatal error. `ignoreCorruptFiles` would take a bare `InternalError` from a reader for a corrupt file, and with a kill pending the executor would report a `NonFatal` wrapper as killed and run on. A pending kill goes out wrapped only around an error the executor's kill case takes, an `InterruptedException` or a `NonFatal` one. Any other error goes out as it is, which for a decoding error is how a plain read raises it. So the reader never runs on after a fatal error. That can stop an executor on a row a plain plan would not have evaluated. The reader also checks for a kill per row group and per chunk of phase 1, since it can run a long way without returning to `FileScanRDD`, which is where a plain read meets one. A key vector only this reader allocates that cannot grow while decoding, which `WritableColumnVector.reserve` reports as a plain `RuntimeException`, gives the filter up for that row group. Any decoding fallback replaces those vectors, so phase 2 allocates what a plain read does. Any failure filling the survivor buffer gives splicing up. That covers a survivor vector that cannot grow. It also covers a key value the filter did not read on that row, such as `b` in `coalesce(a, b)`, since the copy reads every key. Phase 2 then reads the key columns the way a plain read does, so a value that cannot be decoded fails the read only where a plain read fails. A broken invariant fails the task with an internal error that `ignoreCorruptFiles` cannot take for a corrupt file.

Two things can change the answer. The first is `ignoreCorruptFiles`. This reader reads different pages in a different order than a plain read, so which rows survive a corrupt page can differ in either direction. A corrupt non-key page can cost survivors a plain read would have returned, or go unread and keep rows a plain read drops. A corrupt key page is the exception, since giving the row group up meets it at the same batch as a plain read, whether its decoding raises an exception or the codec an `InternalError`, as hadoop-lzo does. The second is a file whose page index is wrong. Returning only the surviving rows of a row group relies on the offset index, so such a file can pair a row's key with another row's values. A read with pushed data filters already relies on the page index, and `parquet.filter.columnindex.enabled=false` turns it off there too. A read with no pushed data filter relies on it only with this feature. The conf doc says both.

**Why does phase 2 splice buffered key values instead of re-reading the key columns?** Re-reading is the simpler design and needs none of the splicing machinery, but it pays a second read of the key columns for every row group. Parquet caches footers rather than pages, so that read goes back to the filesystem. Whether the filesystem serves it without touching the object store depends on the stream. Hadoop 3.5's S3A defaults to the analytics stream, which does buffer, while the classic one does not. Either way the reader asks for those bytes a second time, which is what the measurement below counts.

Measured on a synthetic table of one long key and twenty long payload columns written in 256-row pages. Re-reading transfers 4.7% more bytes than splicing, and 49% more when the projection is the key and one payload column. The comparison that decides it is against the feature being off rather than against splicing. Phase 1 has already read the key column once, so re-reading makes the feature read more than not having it at all, while splicing's worst case reads the column bytes of a plain read. It does take two reads per row group where a plain read takes one, and with no pushed data filter phase 2 also reads the offset indexes of the columns it narrows.

**Why is an all-keys projection not pushed?** A scan whose projected data columns are all key columns of the filter reads exactly the same columns for the same rows as a plain scan, because the reader has to read a key column to evaluate the filter on it, and phase 2 is then left with nothing to prune. All it can add is cost. Phase 1 evaluates the predicate per row through `BasePredicate.eval` on a batch row instead of having it fused into the scan's generated code, the way a post-scan `FilterExec` does, and it copies one value per survivor. So the planner declines that shape, and the reader declines it too rather than carrying a second emit path for it. Making phase 1 evaluate over the key vector is a follow-up, and one of the reasons the conf is off by default.

**Why is the survivor buffer bounded per row group rather than evaluated in chunks?** Phase 1 evaluates a whole row group before the first batch of that row group is emitted, so the survivor vectors are the one thing a task holds that scales with row-group size rather than with the batch capacity. Phase 1 counts the bytes it has buffered and, past `spark.sql.parquet.storageFilterPushdown.maxSplicedRowGroupBytes` (internal, 64MB), releases them and gives splicing up for that row group. Phase 2 then reads every projected column of the surviving rows, so nothing is buffered and the cost is one extra read of the key columns. Evaluating one capacity-sized chunk at a time would bound the memory too, but it turns phase 2 into one read call per chunk, refetches any page that straddles a chunk boundary, and gives up the coalescing and parallelism that a single vectored read gets. What it would shorten is how long the first batch of a row group waits, which is one row group's key decode. The IO is unchanged, since parquet reads a row group's whole requested chunks before it hands back a page store. One smaller per-file cost sits outside that cap. Parquet caches a `ColumnIndexStore` per row group it is asked about, for the life of the file reader, holding an offset index per column the read resolved one for. It is bounded by one file split and freed when the reader closes, it is what parquet's own filtered read path does with a pushed filter too, and bounding it would need a parquet-side change, since the cache is private with no eviction.

**Planning**

- New SQL conf `spark.sql.parquet.storageFilterPushdown.enabled`, default `false`, read by `ParquetFileFormat` rather than by the planner so a Parquet-named conf never decides for another format. It is a planning-time decision, so with it off nothing is attached to a scan and the bloom stays where it is today.
- `FileSourceStrategy.storageFiltersFor` picks the conjuncts to offer from the scan's filters normalized to the relation's column names, the ones the pushed data filters come from, and they go into a new `storageFilters` slot on `FileSourceScanExec` while staying in the `Filter`. Two conditions are per scan, the format's own `supportsStorageFilterPushdown` and `supportBatch` for the schema the reader will see. Three are per conjunct, that it is deterministic, that it references at least one column and only projected data columns, and that the format accepts it. One more is on the set that survives, that at least one projected data column is not a key column, or there is nothing for the reader to prune.
- `FileFormat.supportsStorageFilter(expr)`, defaulting to false, is how the format accepts one of those conjuncts, the same shape as `supportBatch` and `vectorTypes`. The planner keeps what it can see in the plan, which is that the conjunct is deterministic and references only projected columns of this scan, and asks the format about everything to do with its own reader, so the expression shapes and column types a reader supports stay in that reader's package and `FileSourceStrategy` names no format. `ParquetFileFormat` answers true for a top-level `BloomFilterMightContain` over a key type its reader can copy, and false for a column carrying the name of the row-index metadata column, which this reader writes row indexes over. A subclass of itself it excludes one gate earlier, in `supportsStorageFilterPushdown`, since such a subclass may customize reading in a way a storage-filter scan would bypass.
- `FileSourceScanLike` gains the slot, and `FileSourceScanExec.preparedStorageFilters` materializes scalar subqueries and binds the references before the reader is built. The conf is deliberately not rechecked at execution time. A vectorized-reader conf flipped in between makes the reader read plainly rather than fail.

**`FileFormat` API**

- A new `buildReaderWithStorageFilters` takes the filters and the metric map, and returns an `Option`. A format that does not apply them answers `None`, which is the default, and `FileSourceScanExec.inputRDD` then builds an ordinary reader. Declining is safe for the same reason a reader may stop short, that the plan still holds the filter. The `Option` is also what keeps the two builders from being able to call each other, which delegating from the default body would have invited.
- `FileSourceScanExec.inputRDD` routes through the new entry point only when there is something to push, so a `ParquetFileFormat` subclass that customizes `buildReaderWithPartitionValues` keeps working unchanged. That subclass exclusion is asked twice, through one private predicate, in `supportsStorageFilterPushdown` for the planner and again here, since this entry point is reachable without the planner having asked.
- `FileFormat.storageFilterMetrics(sparkContext)` is where the five SQL metrics come from, so the scan node carries them without naming them. What there is to count is the format's own vocabulary, since row groups and page filtering are Parquet's words and another format measures what it avoided differently.

**Parquet reader**

- The read path is a subclass, `LateMaterializationParquetRecordReader`, so the plain one is left where it is. `VectorizedParquetRecordReader` is 615 lines against master's 543, and that difference is seven things. Visibility. The row-group load factored into steps it calls itself. A `newColumnReader` factory, which is where a column reader's rebase and timezone settings are applied. The `rowRanges` parameter `VectorizedColumnReader` gained, with the old constructor kept as an overload. Hadoop's 2-arg `initialize` no longer running `initializeInternal()` a second time after the 5-arg overload it delegates to has run it. A `releaseRowGroupReaders` hook, which drops the installed row group's column readers and row-index iterator. And javadoc. Two of those steps are there for a subclass and do nothing here. `loadNextRowGroup` answers whether it loaded one, which for this class is always yes, since it throws rather than run out of them. `suppliesOwnVector` says a batch slot takes its vector from somewhere other than the row group being installed, which for this class is never. No plain-path logic moved. `nextBatch` and `close` are master's, bar the line that calls the load. It ends up with seven protected methods, five of them new. It calls all of them itself but `releaseRowGroupReaders`, which only the subclass calls, between two row groups. Plus four protected fields, all of which the subclass uses. `ParquetFileFormat` picks the class per scan, so a read with nothing to push is the same read it is today, and a reviewer can check that by diffing the base class and `ParquetReadState` alone.
- The subclass also overrides `nextBatch` and `close`. Its `nextBatch` lets the base read the batch, then points the key slots at that batch's survivors. While splicing, those slots hold survivor vectors rather than the persistent key vectors, so its `close` closes the persistent vectors itself and leaves the base no batch to close. It chains `super.close()` through a `finally`, since that owns the file handle.
- A new `ParquetStorageFilter` holds the bound expression, the key-column indices into the requested schema, the metrics, and the buffer cap below. It releases the expression once it has built its predicate, since a prepared bloom arrives as a binary `Literal` inside that expression while the predicate holds the deserialized filter. That does mean the filter is only ever evaluated on an executor, which is the one thing the driver's copy must not do.
- Three things in the same package are not about this reader and stand on their own. `ValueCopier` holds the per-type copy between column vectors, and is also the single list of key types a filter may use. `ParquetBlockAccounting` holds the footer arithmetic behind the byte metrics and the narrowing decision. `StorageFilterMetrics`'s companion holds the five metrics' keys and labels, so no format code names one.
- Schema evolution is handled without touching the predicate. The row phase 1 evaluates has a slot per key column, and for a key column this file does not have, that slot points at the vector `initBatch` built for it, which holds exactly what the scan will return there, its existence `DEFAULT` or null. So one rule says what a missing column reads as, `ParquetColumnVector`'s, and the filter cannot decide on a value the rows never show. A file missing every key column makes the predicate constant, and it is evaluated once against those vectors. False skips the file, true or an error reads it plainly.
- The row count the reader is told at initialize is the file's before this filter narrows anything. Every phase reads within the rows the pushed data filter kept, the retry after a failed partial read included, so that count stays an upper bound and the base class's terminator is left as it is. A narrowed read ends when the row groups run out, and a file the filter rejects whole sets the count to zero. Whether the page index may be used is read off the same `ParquetReadOptions` the file reader was built with, so that count and the rows phase 0 reads come from one answer.
- `SpecificParquetRecordReaderBase` keeps the `ParquetFileReader` it builds and the options it was built with, which is what lets the three phases switch the requested schema and call `readFilteredRowGroup(blockIdx, rowRanges)`. Both are null for one case, a reader initialized with a `ParquetRowGroupReader` handed in and no file reader behind it, and then the filter is simply not applied.
- `ParquetReadState` has one subclass per way of saying which rows a read includes, every row of the chunk, a range list the caller holds, or the row indexes a page store hands out for filtering parquet did itself. Phase 2 knows the ranges it asked for, so it hands them to the column readers, where before every leaf column of every row group coalesced the same flattened row-index stream back into ranges, and held the whole list while it did. The plain read path keeps the row-index route, since its ranges come from parquet's own column-index filtering, which happens inside the read and produces nothing the caller could have handed over. That route builds its ranges up front, as it always has.
- One owner weighs that budget. Phase 1 checks it after every surviving row, over the buffered key bytes and the row ranges together.
- `parquet.filter.columnindex.enabled` set to false leaves the filter with the row groups it empties, the same degrade a file written with no page index gets. That conf is the escape hatch for a file whose page index is wrong, and phase 2 reads part of a row group through the offset index whatever it says, so honoring it in phase 0 alone would leave a wrong index able to pair a row's key with another row's values.
- Whether a row group can be narrowed at all is asked of the footer before phase 1 buffers anything. Reading part of one goes through the block's column index store, and parquet empties that store altogether if one column it was built over has no offset index. With a pushed data filter that is the whole projection, the store having been built at initialize, so a key column with no offset index is enough to make phase 2 throw. The question is therefore asked of the whole projection. That is stricter than the read needs when no data filter is pushed, where the store would cover the non-key columns alone, and it costs such a row group its page filtering. The shape is a file whose columns do not all carry an offset index, which no writer produces by itself. Parquet's own exception stays as the backstop for the one shape the footer cannot see, an offset index it claims but cannot produce.
- An all-keys projection is declined by the reader as well as by the planner. Such a scan reads the same columns for the same rows either way, so a second emit path for it could only add cost. So is a file that has none of the projected non-key leaves, which under schema evolution only the reader can see.
- The page stores the phases read from are closed by this reader, since parquet closes neither the ones `readFilteredRowGroup` hands back nor the ones from `readNextRowGroup`.
- What planning already guarantees is asserted rather than handled, which is a key ordinal out of range and a non-primitive key column. Five more asserts name an invariant of the read itself, which are no key pages for a block the pushed filter kept, no data pages for one, a page store holding a different number of rows than were asked for, a survivor queue that runs out while the emit loop still has rows, and row ranges handed to a column reader whose pages carry no row indexes to find those rows by. All of them are internal errors, not conditions of a file.

**Metrics.** Five of them, created by the format and only for a scan that has storage filters, all scoped to what the storage filter saved against a read of the same projection without one. A row group whose filter was given up counts nothing, so they can show a saving on a scan that read more than it would have with the feature off. Nor do they take off the offset indexes phase 2 reads for a narrowed row group when no data filter is pushed, which a plain read does not read. Bytes are the compressed bytes the reader did not ask parquet for, which a vectored read may still fetch when it merges nearby ranges.

- `storageFilterRowGroupsSkipped`, "row groups skipped by storage filter", counts row groups whose non-key columns were never read. Phase 1 did read their key columns, unless the file has none of them and the predicate is constant-false over what the scan would return for them, which skips the file whole.
- `storageFilterRowsExcludedByRowGroup`, "rows excluded by storage filter (whole row group)". It counts the rows the pushed data filter's column index kept, so a page that filter drops is not counted.
- `storageFilterRowsExcludedWithinRowGroup`, "rows excluded by storage filter (within row group)". The suffix says where the row was excluded rather than whether reading it was avoided. Such a row may have been read as part of a page that held a survivor, or not read at all because phase 2 skipped its page.
- `storageFilterBytesAvoidedByRowGroup`, "bytes avoided by storage filter (whole row group)".
- `storageFilterBytesAvoidedByPageFiltering`, "bytes avoided by storage filter (page filtering)". A row group that gave splicing up takes its second key read off this, down to zero for that row group.

The byte counters must not cost IO to report, and they do not. The whole-block case answers from the footer's `ColumnChunkMetaData.getTotalSize()`, and a narrower range can only exist where something has already built the block's offset index, so the walk is metadata arithmetic either way. It counts the dictionary page too, since parquet reads that whenever it reads any data page of a chunk, and measures it up to the first data page the offset index names, as parquet's read does. The footer's own first-data-page offset is not used, because parquet-mr 1.11 wrote it pointing at the dictionary page (PARQUET-1977).

### Why are the changes needed?

A runtime bloom filter from join runtime filtering is applied as a post-scan `FilterExec` today. The scan still reads every value page of every row group, even where the bloom drops almost every row immediately. On a selective join over a wide table that read is the dominant cost.

Late materialization turns that around. The scan reads the bloom's key column first, decides which rows survive, and never reads the value pages no surviving row touches. A row group where nothing survives costs one key-column read and no value IO at all.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No change by default, since the conf is off and nothing is attached to a scan in that case.

With the conf on, the following.

- Queries return the same rows. The late-materialization path is exact, and a filter that fails any eligibility check keeps its existing post-scan `FilterExec`. The two exceptions are described above. Under `spark.sql.files.ignoreCorruptFiles`, which rows survive a corrupt page can differ from a plain read, in either direction. And a file whose page index is wrong can pair a row's key with another row's values, which a read with no pushed data filter is exposed to only with this feature.
- `FileSourceScanExec` reports the five metrics above in the SQL UI, and its description gains a `StorageFilters` entry.
- A row group the reader cannot prune is read the way a plain scan reads it, plus one more read of its key columns, since the phase that evaluated the filter has already read them. The query is correct and pays that. A row group with no Parquet page index for one of the projected columns is the case that reaches this, and there the filter is left with the row groups it empties, since narrowing to part of one needs that index. parquet-mr has written the page index since 1.11, but other writers do not, and pyarrow's `write_table` defaults to `write_page_index=False`.
- New `WARN` lines, each at most once per split, which is one reader's share of a file. One reports a row group whose offset index parquet fails to read for a column the read needs. The others report something given up on an error, each in its own line. That is the filter, for a row group or the whole file, after evaluating it or decoding a key page failed. Or it is splicing, after filling the survivor buffer failed. The first carries no stack trace, since parquet has already logged the failed index read with one. The others carry the exception, because that is the error the query would have raised without this feature and it is the user's expression or the file that raised it. A third line reports a byte counter undercounting, which is a should-not-happen diagnostic rather than a shape of a file.
- A consumer that illegally retains a `ColumnarBatch` across `next()` sees a sharper edge than before. The batch object is the same one throughout, as `resultBatch()` documents, but its key slots are rewritten per batch and the vector a previous batch used is freed at the next `nextBatch()`, so with off-heap vectors a retained reference points at released memory rather than stale values. The contract already forbids retaining a batch.
- Phase 1 buffers a whole row group's surviving key values before it produces that row group's first batch. Each reader holds them and their row ranges for one row group at a time. Like the reader's own column vectors, they are not tracked by Spark's memory manager. `spark.sql.parquet.storageFilterPushdown.maxSplicedRowGroupBytes` bounds the values, their per-row overhead and the ranges, not the backing arrays a column vector may grow beyond that.

### How was this patch tested?

New `ParquetStorageFilterSuite`, 121 tests. Four blind review rounds ran over the change before it was opened and seven more since, each by an agent with no knowledge of the earlier ones, and every finding from those and from the reviews on the PR is fixed. Results are compared as ordered or sorted lists rather than sets, so a row returned twice shows.

- Reader-level tests over hand-built filters. Whole row group rejected, with its exact rows and bytes, nothing rejected, mixed in both heap modes, where emitted plus excluded accounts for every row of the file, multi-batch emit, a survivor count that is an exact multiple of the batch capacity, a projection whose key column is not in the leading slot, and an all-keys projection, which the reader declines.
- One case per `ValueCopier` branch across 17 types, with TIME in a test of its own, each in both of the encodings parquet will actually write for it, the variable-length ones also off heap, and each comparing the splicing path against the plain reader over the same file, so values are checked and not only row counts. The encoding is asserted rather than assumed, because asking for a dictionary does not mean getting one. Parquet falls back to PLAIN once the dictionary is no smaller than the values it replaces, and the writer version Spark writes by default has no dictionary writer at all for `BOOLEAN` or for a byte-array `DECIMAL`. Those two and TIME, whose own test writes one file, are the three that get a single encoding. `isSupportedKeyType` and the copier are asserted to agree over a list of 20 supported and 5 unsupported types, which is what the delegation between them makes true by construction.
- Nullable keys, two key columns, two separate storage filters, partition columns alongside spliced keys, off-heap vectors, the row-at-a-time path, `_metadata.row_index`, a complex non-key column, and arrays, maps and arrays of structs read over scattered survivors. Off heap, a spliced batch's key vectors are freed at the next batch. The reader's own vectors and the survivor sets still published or queued are freed at close, and the scratch vectors a decoding fallback replaces are freed at once. A row group's column readers and row indexes are released before the next row group's key columns are read.
- Schema evolution end to end, reading a table whose older file is missing the key column, with a `DEFAULT`, with a `DEFAULT` that fails the filter, with no `DEFAULT` at all, and with one of two key columns missing. Plus a `DEFAULT` that makes the predicate throw, which must read the older file rather than skip it, and an older file that has none of the projected non-key columns, or none of a projected struct's requested fields, which the reader declines and reads plainly.
- Page-level ranges, which need a multi-page row group. Phase 1 stays aligned with the row indexes, and the byte metrics still credit a saving. Asserting they are non-negative would prove nothing, since `SQLMetric` drops a negative. A row group the pushed filter narrowed and the storage filter then emptied counts only the rows the pushed filter kept. Over a filesystem that counts reads, what the plain read transfers more is exactly what the two byte counters report, dictionary pages included.
- Planner gates. The bloom is not offered to the scan when the vectorized reader is unavailable, when the conf is off, when the filter is non-deterministic, and when every projected column is a key column. `supportsStorageFilterPushdown` is asserted with the conf off and on and for a `ParquetFileFormat` subclass, and `supportsStorageFilter` for a plain bloom, a non-bloom predicate, a bloom over an unsupported key type, a cast key, and the trait's default. Offered conjuncts carry the relation's own column names, so a column named like the row-index one is declined in whatever case the query spells it, and a conjunct spelled twice is offered once.
- The ANSI case end to end, with the non-numeric row inside the same row group as matching ones so no statistic prunes it away. The cast key is pushed, the evaluation throws, the row group is given up, and the query returns its rows. Ablating the fail-open makes the same test fail with `CAST_INVALID_INPUT`, which is how the scenario was confirmed rather than assumed. A second case covers an expression that raises a plain JDK error rather than one of Spark's, `timestamp_seconds` of a decimal that does not fit whole microseconds. A third covers a checked `SparkException` from the key expression, the way a Hive UDF raises one, both per row and for the constant of a file missing its key column. Ablating the wider catch fails both. And a pending task kill is rethrown in a form `ignoreCorruptFiles` cannot swallow, and so is an `InternalError` from the expression, a fatal error wrapped inside such an exception goes out as itself, an `AssertionError` falls back like any other error, and a kill that arrives while phase 1 works through a row group is seen at its next chunk. A separate test pins how deep a fatal cause counts, from evaluation and from decoding.
- Extraction preserves results with AQE on and off, and the AQE arm asserts the filter is still on the scan of the final adaptive plan and that the reader excluded rows, since equal results prove nothing there, the post-scan `Filter` guaranteeing them. Canonicalization keeps a storage-filter scan distinct from a plain one, so exchange and subquery reuse cannot cross them. The feature still engages with `ignoreCorruptFiles` on, and its metrics are what say so.
- Every way the reader stops short. A vectorized-reader conf flipped after planning returns every row of the file. A row group whose survivors scatter into more ranges than the cap allows returns that row group whole, whether or not the buffer has already handed a full set of survivors to the queue. And a file with no offset index, built with the low-level `ParquetFileWriter` overloads that take no row count, where its emptied row group is still skipped whole while the others are read whole, and the footer check gets there before the exception path, which the absence of that `WARN` is what asserts. A corrupt key page gives its row group up, and the read then fails at the same batch, after the same rows, as a plain read does. A key vector that cannot grow while decoding, or a codec's `InternalError`, gives its row group up, and the read answers with the next row group filtered again. So does an evaluation error, which gives up its own row group only. A key value the filter does not read on that row and that cannot be decoded, a `b` in `coalesce(a, b)` past a damaged dictionary, gives splicing up, and the read answers. A row group the pushed filter's column index empties while its statistics keep it is passed over, and column-index filtering off keeps the pushed filter's page index unused too. A v2 file's `DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY` decimal column reads right over scattered survivors, which phase 2 skips inside a page and which needed SPARK-59828.
- The survivor cap. Past it the rows are unchanged and the read transfers strictly more bytes, which is what shows the row group really did give splicing up rather than the predicate having been dropped. The byte metric then reports less avoided, for the second key read. A cap of exactly one row group's charge keeps splicing, and one byte less gives it up. And one file whose first row group splices while a later one passes the cap, since the batch is one object and its key slots have to go back to the vectors phase 2 reads into. Each row group's path is asserted there too. And a variable-length key's later accumulator set, which grows as the first one does and is charged per value, plain or dictionary-encoded. A cap of exactly the row group's charge keeps splicing and one byte less gives it up, and every key comes back right on either path. Two key columns are charged together, as long keys and as string keys. On a file of scattered survivors every cap from the row group's charge up splices, so what a row group is charged does not depend on the cap, and a later set's byte child grows as values arrive rather than being sized.
- Whole-stage codegen off, where the planner's gate is weaker than the runtime's, so the bloom is extracted and the spliced batch is served one row at a time. The metrics are what show the row path applied it, since the post-scan `Filter` answers the query either way.
- Column-index filtering off, where the filter keeps only the row groups it empties. The surviving rows' row groups come back whole, the others are skipped, and nothing is excluded inside a row group. The arm with it on returns exactly the surviving rows, so the test cannot pass by the feature being off everywhere.
- A limit under whole-stage codegen, which is the only shape that closes the spliced batch from outside while the reader is still open. The limit makes the row loop leave with a batch still in hand, which is what runs that close.
- `VectorizedRleValuesReaderSuite`'s two row-filtering tests run each read twice, once told the rows as parquet's row indexes and once as the ranges a caller holds next to them, and assert both include the same rows. That is the plain read path's route and the late-materialization one's, over the same positions. A third asserts that ranges with no row indexes are refused.
- And, in one line each: a pushed data filter that drops pages beside a storage filter on the key, each keeping rows the other drops; `create` rejecting a filter that violates a planner precondition; key ordinals collected out of order still pairing with the right batch slots; a non-key column missing from a file, which the byte walks skip; `StorageFilters` appearing in the scan description only when there are some; a format with no storage-filter support declining rather than delegating, and a scan whose format declines returning every row through the ordinary reader; a reader that stops early without draining the file; and Hadoop's 2-arg `initialize` running the reader's initialization once rather than twice.
- A row group whose key column has no offset index is declined by the footer check before phase 1 buffers anything. The file is hand-built for it, with that row group's value column indexed and two later row groups indexed for both columns, which the pushed data filter narrows to one page each. The row group that cannot be narrowed comes back whole, the two that can are still narrowed, and the exception path's `WARN` never fires, because the footer check declines the row group before the read discovers it. Asking the footer about the non-key columns alone fails this test.
- Neither does a row group whose offset index parquet cannot parse, which is the one shape that reaches the phase-2 retry. The same hand-built file is damaged after the fact, its middle row group's key index overwritten while the footer keeps pointing at it, so the footer check passes and the read is what discovers it. The `WARN` has to fire, or the test proves nothing. What it then pins is that the scan reads no more rows than a plain read of the same query, the last row group keeping the pushed filter's page pruning and the row groups around the damaged one keeping the storage filter's own narrowing, since only the damaged one is read again whole.

The oracle is the same scan with no storage filter, so the row indexes and file sizes come from the read.

A filter that keeps every row reads exactly the pages a plain read of the same projection reads, so the two are run over a filesystem that counts every byte handed back and the counts have to match. The walk over the rows the pushed filter kept is covered in both range shapes, the offset-index one and the footer one.

- Pages of a few rows, which wide rows give, make the feature save at every share. The scan alone is 2.0x faster even at 5% scattered.
- Survivors in a contiguous range let whole row groups drop out on every layout. A bloom false positive keeps its row group in, which is why 5% clustered skips fewer row groups on the narrow table.
- Scattered survivors on narrow rows leave little to skip, 34.7 MB at best. There the scan alone takes up to 1.23x the time. This is the shape the gating heuristic in the follow-ups is for.

Possible follow-ups:

- Evaluating the filter over the key column vector rather than per row. The predicate is already compiled, but phase 1 calls it once per row through a row view of the batch, where a post-scan `Filter` has it inlined in the loop that produced the row. That per-row overhead is what an all-keys projection would pay with nothing to gain, so neither the planner nor the reader pushes to one. It is also part of why the conf is off by default.
- Evaluating the filter once per distinct value of a dictionary-encoded key rather than once per row. A verdict per dictionary id, filled the first time the id is seen, turns N evaluations into at most D, which is where a key with many repeats spends most of phase 1. It needs a single key column and a batch that still holds dictionary ids, which a later page falling back to plain encoding ends. It is separate from the item above, which is about the cost of each evaluation rather than how many there are.
- A gating heuristic, so the conf can eventually default to on. The all-keys condition is its trivial first slice, and the rest is projection width against expected selectivity. Scattered survivors are the shape that needs it most, and so is a file without offset indexes. There the filter gains only where a whole row group has no surviving row, a bloom's false positives included, and every other row group reads its key columns twice. Measured on a synthetic table of one long key and twenty long payload columns in 256-row pages, with one survivor every other row, phase 2 skips no page at all and the read takes 5.6x the plain one, because the decode is chopped into one-value calls instead of the vectorized reader's bulk loops. That falls to 1.8x by runs of sixteen rows. A gate cannot be as simple as "no bytes saved, so give up", though. Giving up also re-reads the key columns and hands the post-scan `Filter` every row the filter would have dropped, and those costs grow with what it excluded rather than with what it kept, so the direction flips as the filter gets more selective. It needs a cost model that weighs both, which is why it is here rather than in this PR.
- A vector-to-vector `appendBytes` overload on `WritableColumnVector`, which would remove the per-row `byte[]` that every `ValueCopier` reading `getBinary` allocates, which is strings, binaries and byte-array decimals. It touches the core column-vector classes, so it belongs in its own change.
- Applying the filter inside a row group of a file with no page index, where this PR gives it up because reading part of a row group needs an offset index. Phase 2 could read the whole chunks, which a whole-block `readFilteredRowGroup` already does, and hand the surviving ranges to the column readers, which is how it tells them which rows to read anyway. No bytes would be saved, only decode, so this is the scattered-survivor shape again and wants the same cost model as the gate above. It also needs the emit accounting to take the survivor count rather than the page store's row count.
- Offering the conjuncts that bring in no new column, so a `WHERE k > 100` beside a bloom on `k` is filtered in the reader too, at no extra read. The general form, a prefix of the plan's condition, would also remove the evaluation-order question entirely, but it makes every column the prefix touches a key column, so it needs a cost model rather than a rule.
- Broadcasting the bloom bytes once and sharing the deserialized filter per executor, the way `InSubqueryExec` does. The filter staying in the plan means the task binary now carries it twice, and each task deserializes both. On the row-based path a task also keeps the bytes for its whole life, since the closure captures the scan node, whose storage filters hold them.
- A `PageReadStore.getRowRanges()` in parquet, for the plain read path. The store is built from a `RowRanges` and flattens it into the row-index iterator `ParquetReadState` coalesces back, and only parquet can hand over the ranges there, since its column-index filtering happens inside the read. The late-materialization path already hands its own ranges to the column readers.
- Coarsening the surviving row ranges rather than giving the filter up when their list would pass the budget. Closing a gap shorter than the smallest page row count of the columns phase 2 reads costs no extra bytes, since no page fits wholly inside such a gap, so the filter would keep applying where this PR drops it.
- Releasing a key scratch vector that phase 1 grew for long variable-length keys, once its row group gives splicing or the filter up. Phase 2 then reads those keys into vectors of its own, so both are held. One batch of the longest keys bounds it, so it needs a threshold to be worth the reallocation.
- Accounting the survivor buffer through a `MemoryConsumer` whose `spill()` gives splicing up, so the unified memory manager sees it. The budget counts the values buffered and their per-row overhead, charging a variable-length value four times its length for the byte child's null array and its doubling. A column vector's own capacity is still outside it.
- A counter for row groups whose filter was given up, and for the key bytes read a second time. The five metrics count only what the filter saved, so a scan that read more than it would have with the feature off can still show a saving.
- Separating an error from the filter's own expression from an error in the reader's own code that surfaces while it is evaluated or while the key pages are decoded. Copying a survivor and the reader's invariants already fail loudly. The fallback covers the rest, which keeps every query a plain read answers answerable, but it also turns a bug there into a `WARN` rather than a failed task.
- Making `DataSourceUtils.shouldIgnoreCorruptFileException` answer false while the task is being killed, the way SPARK-50483 and SPARK-50545 made that catch rethrow `BlockMissingException` and `AccessControlException`. A kill that surfaces as an `IOException` from parquet's own reads, such as the `InterruptedIOException` of an interrupted vectored read, is then not taken for a corrupt file under `ignoreCorruptFiles`. A plain read has the same gap, so the fix belongs there and covers every reader.
- Letting the post-scan `Filter` skip the rows the scan already checked, by having the scan return a column that says so. That removes the second evaluation this design pays for, at the price of a synthetic column threaded through the batch and a condition rewrite, and it is the shape the two steps after this one want.

[SPARK-60003][SQL] Do not promote collation-only CAST when applying LCT

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

SPARK-58798 nested every `Cast` when applying string-family LCT so CHAR/VARCHAR truncation and padding stay on the inner node. That is correct when the length constraint changes. For a collation-only change, wrapping `CAST(non-string AS STRING COLLATE x)` makes the outer Cast see a string child, so collation strength is promoted from Default to Implicit. A `CASE` of that CAST next to a UTF8_BINARY literal then becomes Implicit UNICODE, which beats an Implicit column in `concat` and fails CTAS with `INDETERMINATE_COLLATION_IN_SCHEMA`.

This PR:
- Nests Cast only when the CHAR/VARCHAR constraint changes; collation-only LCT retargets with `copy(dataType)` so a non-string CAST stays Default.
- Keeps SPARK-58798 same-collation LCT (`max(n, m)` including mixed Implicit vs Default CHAR).
- Restores the pre-SPARK-58798 Default rule that UTF8_BINARY yields to the other Default collation. Two Implicit columns, or two non-UTF8 Default CASTs, still mismatch.

Does not change CAST collation strength to Implicit.

### Why are the changes needed?

`CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` of `a || ... || CASE ... TRY_CAST(b AS STRING COLLATE UNICODE_CI_AI) ...` fails with `INDETERMINATE_COLLATION_IN_SCHEMA` when `a` is already that collation. The analyzed CASE was Implicit UNICODE vs Default UTF8_BINARY, so CASE became Implicit and then conflicted with concat.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. After SPARK-58798, collation-only LCT wrapping could raise `INDETERMINATE_COLLATION_IN_SCHEMA` on concat/CTAS that previously succeeded. Those queries succeed again. Two Default non-UTF8 collated CASTs still conflict.

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

[SPARK-59784][SQL][TEST] Fix racy waits for SQL execution metrics in tests

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR fixes a racy wait for SQL execution metrics that is shared by several tests, including the flaky `driver side SQL metrics` test in `SQLAppStatusListenerSuite`.

It adds a helper `SharedSparkSession.runAndWaitForExecution(func)`, which drains the listener bus, records the id of the latest execution in the status store, runs `func`, then waits (with `eventually`) until an execution with a larger id has its metrics computed, and returns that id. It is used in:
- `SharedSparkSession.runAndFetchMetrics` (used by `InMemoryTableMetricSuite` and `KeyGroupedPartitioningSuite`)
- `SQLAppStatusListenerSuite`: `driver side SQL metrics`, `SPARK-34338: Report metrics from Datasource v2 scan`, `SPARK-39635: Report driver metrics from Datasource v2 scan`, `SPARK-36030: Report metrics from Datasource v2 write`
- `PythonDataSourceSuite`: `SPARK-46424: Support Python metrics`
- `PythonUDFSuite`: `SPARK-34265: Instrument Python UDF execution using SQL Metrics` and `SPARK-55046: pythonProcessingTime metric is available for Python UDFs`

It also removes an unused execution count from `InMemoryTableMetricSuite`.

`SPARK-37578: Update output metrics from Datasource v2` in `SQLAppStatusListenerSuite` and `BasicWriteJobStatsTrackerMetricSuite` still wait on execution counts. This is on purpose: the first reads task output metrics from its own listener, and the second uses its own local session where it expects exactly two executions, so neither reads the metrics of the latest execution by id.

### Why are the changes needed?

`driver side SQL metrics` fails intermittently in CI, e.g. in the scheduled master and branch-4.x builds:

```
- driver side SQL metrics *** FAILED *** (21 milliseconds)
  Map(3105033 -> "2", 3105032 -> "1", 3105031 -> "total (min, med, max (stageId: taskId))
  0 ms (0 ms, 0 ms, 0 ms (stage 5.0: task 10))") did not contain key 3105125 (SQLAppStatusListenerSuite.scala:607)
```

The tests above wait for the metrics of the execution they just ran like this:
1. Wait for `executionsCount() < oldCount` to become false (or for `executionsCount() >= oldCount` to hold). This is always satisfied immediately, since the count never drops below the count taken before the query.
2. Wait until `executionsList().last.metricValues != null`, then read the metrics of `executionsList().last`.

`SQLAppStatusListener` processes events asynchronously. If it has not processed the new execution yet, `executionsList().last` is an older execution, e.g. from a previous test, which already has metric values. The wait then ends immediately and the test reads the wrong execution's metrics. The map in the failure above is such a previous execution's metrics. The two `PythonUDFSuite` tests read `executionsList().last` without waiting at all.

Waiting for a larger execution id rather than a larger execution count is needed because the status store evicts old executions once `spark.sql.ui.retainedExecutions` is reached, after which the count no longer grows. Execution ids always grow.

In addition, several of the old waits were unbounded `while` / `Thread.sleep` loops, so a real hang would never fail the test.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Test-only change.

### How was this patch tested?

- Reproduced the race deterministically with a temporary (not included) suite that stalls the status listener queue for 2 seconds while the query runs: the old wait logic (both the `SQLAppStatusListenerSuite` loops and the old `runAndFetchMetrics`) fails every time with the same symptom as CI (it reads the previous execution's metrics), and `runAndWaitForExecution` passes.
- Reproduced the baseline race from review deterministically with a temporary (not included) suite that keeps an earlier execution's events queued while the baseline is read: without draining the listener bus first, `runAndWaitForExecution` returns that earlier execution; with it, it returns the execution `func` ran.
- Verified with a temporary (not included) suite that `runAndWaitForExecution` works when the status store is at its retention limit (`spark.sql.ui.retainedExecutions=2`).
- Ran all affected suites locally, all passed: `SQLAppStatusListenerWithInMemoryStoreSuite`, `SQLAppStatusListenerWithRocksDBBackendSuite`, `InMemoryTableMetricSuite`, `KeyGroupedPartitioningSuite`, `PythonDataSourceSuite` and `PythonUDFSuite` (the Python suites with pandas and pyarrow installed, so no test was skipped).

[SPARK-58814][SQL] Cover CHAR/VARCHAR round-trips and stop ORC truncating scans

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Under `spark.sql.charVarchar.standardSemantics.enabled`, CHAR/VARCHAR
round-trip through the major file formats (Parquet, ORC, Avro, CSV,
JSON), including nested fields.

Length enforcement follows the physical type:

- Native CHAR/VARCHAR in the file (for example Hive-written ORC
  char(n)/varchar(n)): the data source enforces padding and length.
- STRING in the file with a Spark CHAR/VARCHAR schema: Spark enforces
  (`EXCEED_LIMIT_LENGTH` on overflow, CHAR padding).

Spark's ORC writer stores CHAR/VARCHAR as ORC STRING plus
`spark.sql.catalyst.type` metadata. The ORC reader asks for STRING and
Spark applies the CHAR/VARCHAR constraints. Native ORC CHAR/VARCHAR
already in a file stay ORC's responsibility.

### Why are the changes needed?

Standard-semantics CHAR/VARCHAR must survive file write/read as first-class
types, and STRING columns read with a Spark CHAR/VARCHAR schema must use
Spark's length checks.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes.

For unreleased standard-semantics CHAR/VARCHAR:

- File sources keep CHAR/VARCHAR schemas and values when the flag is on.
- A STRING ORC column read as CHAR/VARCHAR is checked by Spark. Over-length
  values raise `EXCEED_LIMIT_LENGTH`.
- Native ORC CHAR/VARCHAR are enforced by ORC.

For the released `spark.sql.preserveCharVarcharTypeInfo` path:

[SPARK-59933][SQL] Eliminate quadratic nested field aliasing deduplication

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
Within any expression, there can be multiple nested struct read subexpressions (ex. read `a.b.c`, `a.b`, and `a.d`). All of these are independent candidates for column aliasing, and `NestedColumnAliasing.getAttributeToExtractValues` is responsible for dropping read expressions that are nested anywhere beneath another read. Ex. instead of aliasing `a.b.c` and `a.b` independently, we should only alias `a.b` and then reuse that alias as `some_alias.c`

But `NestedColumnAliasing` achieves this by iterating over every nested read subexpression, and comparing it against every other read subexpression for semantic equality on its ancestor.

This is quadratic with respect to the number of nested field read subexpressions, which can be noticeable for plans constructed against large (wide/deep) tables, especially generated ones. Two behavior-preserving optimizations are proposed:

1. Build an `ExpressionSet` of the reads once and look up each parent node in it. This is equivalent to `semanticEquals`. `ExpressionSet` stores only deterministic expressions in canonical form and canonicalizes the queried expression, so a match requires both expressions to be deterministic with equal canonical forms.
2. Plans often repeat the same read many times, so deduplicate with `.distinct` before filtering rather than after, to avoid repeated work. The result is the same, because removing exact duplicates doesn't change which reads are semantically present.

For typical small plans, the overhead is negligible - the previous `semanticEquals` comparisons already canonicalized every read, so the only added work is building a small hash set.

### Why are the changes needed?
Improve nested field read aliasing performance.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
No. This is a pure optimization that should not introduce any behavioral change.

### How was this patch tested?
No new logic is added, but added tests to bring coverage for existing untested contracts (non-deterministic but identically canonicalized plans are still aliased separately, and deterministic plans that are canonically the same are indeed considered for shared-aliasing).

[SPARK-59929][SQL] Fail fast when a window partition exceeds Int.MaxValue rows

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`org.apache.spark.sql.execution.ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray` counted the buffered rows of a
window partition in a 32-bit `Int` (`numRows`), exposed via `def length: Int`. When a single
window partition exceeds `Int.MaxValue` (2,147,483,647) rows, the counter overflows and wraps
negative, which silently corrupts the window-frame logic that reads it (most visibly, `lag`/`lead`
returning `NULL` for every row; an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` is the sibling symptom at larger
sizes).

Window execution tracks the per-row index and window bounds in 32-bit `Int`s at several layers --
the row counter above, the row index the driver (`WindowEvaluatorFactory` /
`ArrowWindowPythonEvaluatorFactory`) passes to `WindowFunctionFrame.write`, the per-frame bounds,
and the row accounting inside the spill-backed `UnsafeExternalSorter.getIterator`. Making window
functions produce correct results over partitions larger than `Int.MaxValue` rows therefore
requires widening all of these, which is a large change (notably the core sorter accounting, see
the follow-up below).

This PR takes the contained, safe step: it detects the condition and fails fast with a clear error
rather than silently returning wrong results.

- Widens the row counter and its accessor to `Long` (`numRows`/`length` in
  `ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray`) so the true partition size can be observed instead of a
  wrapped negative value. `QueryExecutionErrors.invalidStartIndexError` is widened accordingly.
- Adds a guard, `WindowEvaluatorFactoryBase.checkPartitionSizeLimit`, called by both window drivers
  after a partition is buffered. If the partition has more than `Int.MaxValue` rows it throws the
  new error condition `WINDOW_FUNCTION_PARTITION_SIZE_EXCEEDS_LIMIT` (SQLSTATE `54000`).
- Uses `Math.toIntExact` at the remaining 32-bit narrowing sites in the frames and in
  `WindowSegmentTree` as a defensive backstop that fails loudly rather than truncating silently.

Making the offset frames (`lag`/`lead`, unbounded-offset `nth_value`) actually produce correct
results over such partitions requires widening the `UnsafeExternalSorter` row accounting to `Long`
and is tracked as a follow-up:
[SPARK-59941](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59941). Until then every window frame is
guarded.

This is the read-path counterpart of the write/insertion-path overflow fixed by
[SPARK-51757](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-51757), which did not widen
`numRows`/`length`.

### Why are the changes needed?

Window queries over a single partition larger than `Int.MaxValue` rows can return silently
incorrect results. The clearest case, confirmed by reproduction, is `lag`/`lead` returning `NULL`
for every row:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS n_rows, max(prev) AS max_prev, max(id) AS max_id
FROM (
  SELECT id, lag(id, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY CAST(0 AS INT) ORDER BY id) AS prev
  FROM range(2200000000)
);
```

```
n_rows   = 2200000000     (all rows funnel to ONE partition via PARTITION BY a constant)
max_prev = NULL           <-- BUG. Correct value is 2199999998
max_id   = 2199999999     (sanity: the range itself is intact)
```

`lag(id, 1)` over ids `0..2199999999` must yield `NULL, 0, 1, ..., 2199999998`, so `max(prev)` must
be `2199999998`; it returned `NULL` for every row. A query should either produce a correct result
or fail with a clear error, never silently return wrong data.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. A window query over a partition larger than `Int.MaxValue` rows now fails with the new error
condition `WINDOW_FUNCTION_PARTITION_SIZE_EXCEEDS_LIMIT` (SQLSTATE `54000`) instead of silently
returning wrong results (e.g. `lag`/`lead` returning `NULL` for every row) or throwing an
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Partitions up to and including `Int.MaxValue` rows are unaffected.

### How was this patch tested?

- New `WindowFunctionFrameSuite`: the partition-size guard allows `Int.MaxValue` rows and rejects
  anything larger with the expected error condition and message parameter.
- New test in `ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArraySuite` pinning `length` as a `Long`.
- Regression: `DataFrameWindowFunctionsSuite` and `WindowSegmentTreeSuite` pass unchanged;
  `SparkThrowableSuite` validates the new error condition.

Materializing a 2^31+ row partition in a unit test is infeasible (the manual reproduction above
took ~30 minutes over 2.2B rows on a dedicated core), so the overflow boundary is covered by the
targeted unit tests above rather than an end-to-end run.
